newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe launches Commercial Bank privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe launches Commercial Bank privatisation.

text.p: The government of Zimbabwe launched on Wednesday its sale of 80 percent of the shares in the Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe, lending further impetus to the state privatisation programme.

The state is offering 320 million shares at Z$1.60 each in a move aimed at raising Z$512 million ($44 million), Z$250 million of which will be used to recapitalise the bank to comply with central Reserve Bank capital adequacy requirements.
Local regulations require banks to operate within a prescribed minimum risk-weighted ratio of eight percent. The CBZ's capital adequacy ratio is currently at one percent.
This use of funds is in stark contrast to the government's privatisation at the end of June of the national dairy, Dairibord Zimbabwe, where proceeds from the sale went into state coffers.
According to the privatisation prospectus, about Z$92 million of the cash raised will fund an expansion scheme, including computerisation and extension of branches across the southern African state.
The remainder would be used to increase the number and value of its transactions.
CBZ managing director Gideon Gono told prospective investors on Wednesday the capital raised would not be used to cover funding of its bad debts, recently transferred to a new firm, CBZ Nominees.
CBZ's accumulated non-performing loan portfolio stood at Z$599.1 million as at December 31, 1996.

"The new capital being sought is not going towards the funding of this (bad debt) book and any administrative arrangements between CBZ Nominees and the bank is on an 'arms-length' and commercial basis," Gono said.

Local institutions such as pension funds and insurance firms will hold 27 percent of the share capital, individuals and the state National Investment Trust 26 percent, and an as yet unidentified partner will hold a 25 percent stake.
The bank's employees will hold the remaining two percent.
The offer opens on Thursday, August 7 and closes August 29.
Gono told Reuters that shareholders would decide at an extraordinary general meeting due before April 8 whether the share would be listed on the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange.
Local stock market officials were bullish about the CBZ offer, saying it was likely to be as successful as the Dairibord issue which was 10 times oversubscribed.

"I'm optimistic this will be a success...The timing is wise, it's coming in when the (Zimbabwe stock) market is at all time highs, scrip is very short, there's a lot of cash in the system," ZSE chairman Mark Tunmer told Reuters.
The privatisation is being sponsored by four local brokers, Kingdom Stockbrokers, Remo Investment Brokers, Intermarket Stockbrokers and Continental Securities Trading.
